planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions in spring into constantly moist, gritty soil in part shade to full sun; Parry's Primrose needs the cold, running-water conditions of an alpine seep to thrive.

directions: Plant in part shade to full sun in constantly moist, gritty soil, mimicking the alpine snowmelt rivulets and wet seeps above 10,000 feet where it grows naturally. Parry's Primrose bears striking magenta flowers with a yellow eye on scapes to 16 inches, blooming June through August, with foliage carrying a notably strong, skunk-like scent that is unmistakable in the field. It needs a bog garden, pond margin, or alpine trough with constant water movement to succeed outside its native high-elevation habitat, and is a genuine showpiece for a dedicated alpine wetland planting.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall near established grasses or sedges in consistently wet soil in full to part sun; Elephanthead Lousewort is hemiparasitic on grass and sedge roots, so it establishes best sown directly among them rather than transplanted.

directions: Direct sow near established grass or sedge roots in consistently wet soil in full to part sun; Elephanthead Lousewort is hemiparasitic, tapping into the roots of neighboring grasses and sedges for part of its nutrition, which makes it best sown directly into an existing wet meadow or fen planting rather than transplanted as a potted specimen. Its distinctive pink flower spikes, each bloom shaped remarkably like a tiny elephant's head with trunk and ears, appear from July through August in subalpine and alpine fens and wet meadows. Give it a permanent wet-meadow companion planting rather than isolating it alone.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions in spring into constantly moist soil in part shade; Fringed Grass-of-Parnassus needs cold, running water conditions typical of an alpine fen or streambank.

directions: Plant in part shade in constantly moist soil, the alpine and subalpine fen and streambank conditions it favors naturally. Fringed Grass-of-Parnassus bears delicate white flowers with distinctively fringed petal margins on stems 6-12 inches tall, blooming late in the season from July through September. It is a good choice for a bog garden or pond-edge planting at the cooler end of its hardiness range, where its late bloom extends interest after many other alpine wetland species have finished.
sources: Rocky Mountain native wetland plant specialty nurseries

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring into gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; Netleaf Willow forms a prostrate mat suited to a trough, scree, or alpine rock garden.

directions: Plant in full sun in gritty, well-drained soil; Netleaf Willow is a prostrate krummholz shrub reaching only about 4 inches tall, forming dense mats of rounded, deeply veined leaves at timberline and along alpine turf edges. Small catkins appear in early summer. Its diminutive scale and tolerance of harsh alpine exposure make it a favorite among rock-garden and trough enthusiasts for representing true timberline dwarfing in a garden setting, far more compact than any lowland willow.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into lean, sharply drained, rocky soil in full sun; Bristlecone Pine is extremely slow-growing, well suited to a specimen planting or bonsai culture.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, rocky soil in full sun; Bristlecone Pine is the iconic timberline krummholz conifer of the Rocky Mountains, growing naturally at 9,500 to 12,000 feet elevation and famous for extreme longevity, with wild specimens reaching thousands of years old. Needles grow in bundles of five, flecked with distinctive white resin dots, on an extremely slow-growing tree widely used in landscape and bonsai cultivation well beyond its native habitat range. It tolerates poor, rocky soil and harsh exposure far better than richer garden conditions, and is hardy well beyond zone 7 in cultivation.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions in spring into moist, gritty soil in full sun; King's Crown needs the cold, consistently wet conditions of an alpine seep despite its succulent leaves.

directions: Plant in full sun in moist, gritty soil, the alpine and subalpine seep and fen-margin habitat it favors naturally despite its succulent, water-storing leaves. King's Crown forms a clump of fleshy foliage topped by dense, striking rose-red flower heads from July through August, a notable color departure from the more common yellow-flowered Rhodiola species already in cultivation. It is a genuine showpiece for an alpine bog garden or pond margin where constant cool moisture can be maintained.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into consistently wet soil in full sun to part shade; Star Gentian is a circumboreal species also native to Colorado's subalpine fens.

directions: Plant in full sun to part shade in consistently wet soil; Star Gentian bears blue-purple, fringed, star-shaped flowers with visible nectar glands on stems 8-20 inches tall, blooming in midsummer across wet subalpine and alpine meadows and fens. It is a circumboreal species, also found across northern Europe and Asia, and is well suited to a bog garden or pond-margin planting that can maintain the cool, constant moisture it needs. Its fringed, star-like flower form sets it apart from more typical trumpet-shaped gentians already in cultivation.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into acidic, consistently wet soil in full sun to part shade; Alpine Bog Laurel is sometimes still listed under the name Kalmia polifolia var. microphylla.

directions: Plant in full sun to part shade in acidic, consistently wet soil; Alpine Bog Laurel is a dwarf evergreen shrub reaching only about 10 inches, bearing small pink saucer-shaped flowers in early summer. It grows in subalpine and alpine fens, bogs, and the wet turf fringing the krummholz zone, and is sometimes still catalogued under its older name, Kalmia polifolia var. microphylla. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, consistent with other Kalmia species, so site it with that in mind. It needs a bog garden or consistently saturated acidic bed to thrive outside its native high-elevation habitat.
sources: Ericaceous and native bog-plant specialty nurseries

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Entire-Leaf Mountain Avens is distinguished from the already-present Dryas octopetala by its smooth-margined, non-lobed leaves.

directions: Plant in full sun in lean, well-drained soil; Entire-Leaf Mountain Avens is a mat-forming subshrub reaching only about 4 inches tall, distinguished from the already-grown Dryas octopetala by its glossy, smooth-margined leaves rather than the lobed foliage of its relative. Cream-white, eight-petaled flowers in spring give way to feathery, plumed seed heads that persist attractively into summer. It occupies alpine turf and the talus fringing the krummholz zone, making an excellent groundcover for an alpine rock garden or trough.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions in spring into gritty, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Snowball Saxifrage blooms very early, often right at the snowmelt edge.

directions: Plant in full sun to part shade in gritty, moist, well-drained soil; Snowball Saxifrage forms a basal rosette topped by dense, rounded clusters of small white flowers on stems 4-10 inches tall, blooming very early in the season, often right at the retreating edge of snowmelt from May through July. It occupies alpine turf, scree margins, and subalpine meadows, making it a good early-season companion to other alpine rock-garden plants. Availability is somewhat thinner than other alpine species in this group, generally found through specialty alpine nurseries and regional native-plant sales rather than general retail.
